teaser: Christ is being whipped in the back room. In front, three men stand talking. Nobody knows why.
review_notes:
Panel about 58 x 81 cm; date uncertain (proposals range from the 1440s to about 1470); metadata says 1460.
Signature reads OPVS PETRI DE BVRGO SCI SEPVLCRI.
Vanishing point placed by eye from the ceiling beams and the right-hand colonnade: low, near the legs of the man in green. The drawn lines are approximate.
Pilate's hat resembling that of the Byzantine emperor John VIII Palaiologos (as on Pisanello's medal): standard observation.
Theories cited: Oddantonio da Montefeltro (murdered 1444) with two advisers; Cardinal Bessarion and the fall of Constantinople (1453). Presented as theories.
Lost frame inscription 'Convenerunt in unum' recorded in the 19th century.
Theft from the Ducal Palace of Urbino in February 1975, recovery in Locarno, Switzerland, in March 1976.
'The greatest small painting in the world' is attributed to Kenneth Clark.
Second light source inside the hall (bright ceiling bay above Christ, lit from the right) follows Marilyn Lavin's reading.

lesson.text: The title promises violence: a man tied to a column and whipped. Yet this may be the calmest picture you will ever see. And the victim, the most important person in the Christian story, is small and far away, while three strangers who are not even watching take up the front.

It is small in fact, too. The wooden panel measures about 58 by 81 centimeters (23 by 32 inches), the size of a carry-on suitcase lid. Piero della Francesca painted it for someone in or near Urbino, a hill town in central Italy. Who ordered it, and for what, is lost.

The picture splits down the middle. On the left, a cool marble hall, seen deep. On the right, an open square under blue sky, seen close. A white column stands between them like the gutter of an open book. Piero built this double space with ruler-straight logic.
Three lines show how the picture is engineered.

lines.label: The divide
lines.text: This column cuts the panel into two worlds. Nothing crosses it: no glance, no gesture, no shadow. The men outside behave as if the hall did not exist.

lines.label: A ceiling beam
lines.text: The dark beam overhead runs straight into depth. Extend it and it dives to a point low in the picture, near the legs of the man in green.

lines.label: The colonnade
lines.text: The row of columns on the right side of the hall shrinks toward that same low point. Every receding edge of the building agrees on it.

lesson.text: That meeting place is the vanishing point, the spot where lines running away from you appear to join. Piero sets it very low, at about knee height. So we see the hall from below, as if we were sitting or kneeling, and the architecture rises above us, tall and solemn.

Piero was a working mathematician. He wrote a manual of arithmetic for merchants, a book on geometric solids, and one of the first treatises on perspective for painters. For centuries after his death he was better remembered for the math than for the pictures.

The space is so exact that scholars have measured it and drawn the floor plan of the hall, tile by tile, as if it were a real building. Inside that precise box, Piero places five figures and a statue. Each one has been argued over.

lesson.title: The back room
lesson.text: Walk in from the left, where the judge sits.

spots.title: The judge
spots.text: Pontius Pilate, who ordered the whipping, sits in pink and blue. His pointed hat copies that of the Byzantine emperor of the day. On the step under his chair, in capitals, is Piero's signature.

spots.title: The man in a turban
spots.text: He stands barefoot with his back to us, one hand open, watching. We never see his face. The turban marked him, for Italian viewers, as a man from the East.

spots.title: Christ
spots.text: Pale, nearly naked, hands tied behind him at a column. Two men raise their whips, but no stroke lands and his skin is unmarked. The punishment is frozen before it starts.

spots.title: The golden idol
spots.text: On top of the column stands a small gold statue of a nude man holding up a silvery ball, a pagan god or emperor. It gleams above Christ's head: old Rome, shining over the man it condemns.

lesson.text: No blood, no cry, no crowd. The whips hang in the air like hands on a stopped clock. Even the light is odd: the square outside is lit from the left, but the ceiling panel above Christ glows as if a second, hidden light shone inside the hall.
Piero turns a scene of torture into a still, measured vision. The geometry is not decoration: its calm order is the mood of the picture.

Now the foreground. Three men stand in a loose triangle on red tiles. A bearded one in a dark hat seems to speak. An older, shaved-headed one in blue and gold brocade listens. Between them stands a youth who does not fit, and his feet tell you so.
Two of the three men outside wear shoes or boots. One does not. Find the bare feet.

spots.title: Barefoot on the tiles
spots.text: The blond youth in the plain red robe stands barefoot, like Christ in the hall behind him. No hat, no jewels, eyes fixed on nothing. He looks less like a guest than like an apparition.

lesson.text: Who is he? One old theory says a young ruler of Urbino, murdered in 1444, standing between the advisers who ruined him. Another makes the bearded man a Greek envoy pleading for help after Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1453, with Christ's suffering standing for that of the Eastern church. Others see an angel.

The old frame, now lost, reportedly carried three Latin words: “Convenerunt in unum,” “they came together.” The phrase comes from a psalm read on Good Friday about rulers uniting against Christ. It is a clue, and it settles nothing.

Dozens of explanations have been published, and none has won. Piero signed the panel proudly and explained nothing. Perhaps the first owner needed no explanation, because he knew the three faces personally. We are reading a private message with the key missing.
In February 1975 thieves broke into the palace museum in Urbino at night and left with this panel and two other paintings. All three were recovered the following year in Switzerland.

The British art historian Kenneth Clark is credited with calling it the greatest small painting in the world. The beginning contradiction is still there for every visitor: a whipping that makes no sound, and three men with their backs to it, whose conversation we will never overhear.

quiz.question: What separates the two halves of the picture?
quiz.explanation: A column divides the marble hall from the open square.

quiz.question: Where does Piero place the vanishing point?
options: Very low, near knee height in the hall
quiz.explanation: The low point makes us see the hall from below.

quiz.question: What stands on top of the column Christ is tied to?
options: A golden statue holding a ball
quiz.explanation: A small gold pagan figure gleams above Christ's head.

quiz.question: What sets the blond youth apart from the two men beside him?
options: He is barefoot and plainly dressed
quiz.explanation: He stands barefoot in a simple red robe between two richly dressed men.

quiz.question: Besides painting, what was Piero known for?
quiz.explanation: He wrote books on arithmetic, geometry and perspective.

facts.text: Historians agree on exactly who the three men in the foreground are.
facts.explanation: Dozens of theories exist and none has been accepted by everyone.

facts.text: The painting was stolen in 1975 and recovered the next year.
facts.explanation: Thieves took it from Urbino and it was found in Switzerland.

facts.text: Christ's body is shown covered in wounds from the whips.
facts.explanation: No stroke has landed and his skin is unmarked.
